blocks.text: AI 年复一年地不断刷新各项新基准。然而，即便 AI 超越人类的基准清单持续增长，AI 实际的经济影响似乎增长得更慢。

blocks.text: 这种“生产力悖论”反映了基准测试的几个事实：它们通常被校准为衡量前沿 AI 相较过去能力的进步（而非与人类表现对比）；它们往往局限于性能易于评分的任务；而且 AI 有时会针对基准进行训练，就像高中生被教导应对 SAT 一样。所有这些都造成了 AI 在基准上的得分与其在现实世界中实际能力之间的差距。

blocks.text: 要更好地理解 AI 距离胜任真实人类工作还有多远，我们需要弥合这一差距的方法。

blocks.text: 去年二月，Epoch 高级研究员 Anson Ho 尝试将自己的工作自动化，测试 AI 能在哪些任务上胜任——又在哪些地方力有不逮。答案是：它在所有任务上都失败了，但他预测到本十年末情况将不再如此。

inlines.text: 最近，我们将这一初步尝试扩展为 Epoch 自动化报告，汇集了我们在 Epoch 定期执行的一系列任务，例如平面设计和研究项目规划，并按照我们对人类工作的同等标准来评估 AI。

blocks.text: 在这些任务上评估 AI 比大多数标准基准更费功夫，但更能代表真实工作的挑战：它们要求模型收集上下文、使用工具，并处理 Epoch 人类员工所面对的复杂性。

blocks.text: 那么，模型表现如何？

inlines.text: 那么，模型表现如何？

blocks.text: 领先的 Claude Fable 5.1 和 GPT-6 Astra 平均得分 65%。这意味着它们的产出满足了人类员工将被评估的评分标准中 65% 的条目——100% 的得分意味着该任务可以放心自动化。

blocks.text: 65% 的得分仍然意味着任务失败

inlines.text: 65% 的得分仍然意味着任务失败

blocks.text: 这些结果并不一定意味着我们在时间或任务难度上已走完自动化的 65%，尽管领先的 AI 能达到 Epoch 人类员工所需质量的 65%。

inlines.text: 这些结果并不一定意味着我们在时间或任务难度上已走完自动化的 65%，尽管领先的 AI 能达到 Epoch 人类员工所需质量的 65%。

blocks.text: 首先，这些分数可能反映的是在较容易的评分条目上的成功。例如，AI 能生成有前景的研究方向，但在创建可执行实验这一更难的任务上却举步维艰。在进行一项试点实验时，GPT-6 Astra 为其评估的模型设置的 token 预算过低，导致 22% 的运行无法返回任何答案。但它随后将这些失败视为关于模型能力的关键发现，而非设置缺陷。

blocks.text: 总体而言，AI 在定义明确的任务（如编码和数据分析）上表现更好，在开放式任务（如从示例中归纳模式以及涉及判断的任务）上表现更差。当被要求设计一张图形并提供许多 Epoch 风格的示例时，Fable 5.1 生成了一张杂乱无章的图表，塞满了过多信息，无法有效传达。相比之下，接受同一任务的 Epoch 设计师提供了一张简洁清晰的图表。

blocks.text: 这些发现为经济影响为何滞后提供了一种可能的解释——65% 还不够。如果人类提交了这些任务中的任何一个，都会被拒绝或修改。虽然这样的产出可能有帮助，但仍需要人类来评估并修正每一个错误。但随着 AI 不断进步，它将在更多任务上越过 100% 的门槛，届时人类就会把该任务交给 AI。

blocks.text: 在这项评估中，已经有一个任务出现了这种情况。我们移除了一个基础的图表生成任务，因为 Fable 5.1 大多数时候能在一次尝试中生成可接受的图表。Epoch 现在已在我们日常工作中部分自动化了这一步骤。随着 AI 在更多任务上达到人类质量阈值，我们预计会看到更多的经济影响。

blocks.text: AIs continue to saturate new benchmarks year after year. Yet even as the list of benchmarks where AI has surpassed humans keeps growing, the actual economic impact of AI seems to be growing more slowly.

inlines.text: AIs continue to saturate new benchmarks year after year. Yet even as the list of benchmarks where AI has surpassed humans keeps growing, the actual
economic impact
of AI seems to be growing more slowly.

blocks.text: This “productivity paradox” reflects several facts about benchmarks: they are often calibrated to measure cutting-edge AI progress compared to past capabilities (rather than against human performance); they are often limited to tasks where performance can be easily graded; and AIs are sometimes trained to the benchmark, like a high school student being taught to the SAT. All of these create a gap between how an AI scores on benchmarks and what it can actually do in the real world.

All of these create a gap between how an AI scores on benchmarks and what it can actually do in the real world.

blocks.text: To better understand how close AI is to doing real human jobs, we need ways to close that gap.

inlines.text: To better understand how close AI is to doing real human jobs, we need ways to close that gap.

blocks.text: Last February, Epoch senior researcher Anson Ho attempted to automate away his job, testing where AI could handle his tasks — and where it fell short. The answer: It failed all of the tasks, but he forecast that wouldn’t be the case by the end of the decade.

blocks.text: Recently, we expanded that initial effort into the Epoch Automation Reports, a collection of tasks we do regularly at Epoch, such as graphic design and planning research projects, on which we evaluate AI according to the same standards we expect of human work.

blocks.text: Evaluating AI on these tasks is more work than most standard benchmarks, but better represents the challenges of real work: They require models to gather context, use tools, and handle the complexity that Epoch’s human workers face.

blocks.text: So, how did the models do?

inlines.text: So, how did the models do?

blocks.text: The leaders, Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra, scored 65% on average. That means their output met 65% of the rubric items that human employees would be evaluated on — a score of 100% would mean that it’s fine to automate the task.

blocks.text: A 65% score is still a failed task

inlines.text: A 65% score is still a failed task

blocks.text: These results don’t necessarily mean we’re 65% of the way towards automation in terms of time or task difficulty, even though leading AIs can achieve 65% of the quality required from a human Epoch employee.

inlines.text: These results don’t necessarily mean we’re 65% of the way towards automation in terms of time or task difficulty, even though leading AIs can achieve 65% of the quality required from a human Epoch employee.

blocks.text: For starters, these scores might reflect success on easier rubric items. For example, AIs can generate promising research directions, but struggle on the harder task of creating actionable experiments. When carrying out a pilot experiment, GPT-6 Astra set the token budget too low for the models it was evaluating, so that 22% of runs were unable to return any answer. But it then treated these failures as a key finding about model capabilities, rather than a setup flaw.

blocks.text: In general, the AIs did better at clearly defined tasks (e.g. coding and data analysis), and worse at open-ended ones (e.g. picking up patterns from examples and tasks that involve judgment). When asked to design a graphic and provided many examples of Epoch’s style, Fable 5.1 produced a cluttered graph crammed with too much information to communicate effectively. In contrast, an Epoch designer given the task provided a clean, simple chart.

blocks.text: These findings give a possible explanation for why economic impact lags — 65% isn’t sufficient. Every one of those tasks would be rejected or revised if a human had submitted it. While such outputs can be helpful, they still require a human to evaluate and fix each mistake. But as AI continues to get better, it will tip over the 100% threshold for more tasks, and then the humans will hand that task over to the AI.

blocks.text: This has already happened with one task in this evaluation. We removed a basic chart-generation task because Fable 5.1 is able to produce an acceptable chart in one try most of the time. Epoch now partly automates this step in our daily work. As AI hits human-quality thresholds for more tasks, we expect to see a lot more economic impact.
